p.hi: The Action takes place at Kenyon-Fulton, Claude Insoley’s place in Somersetshire.

div.head: THE FIRST ACT
div.p: Scene: The drawing-room at Kenyon-Fulton. It is a handsome apartment with large windows, reaching to the ground. On the walls are old masters whose darkness conceals their artistic insignificance. The furniture is fine and solid. Nothing is very new or smart. The chintzes have a rather pallid Victorian air. The room with its substantial magnificence represents the character of a family rather than the taste of an individual.

p.hi: It is night and one or two electric lamps are burning.

div.p: Moore, an elderly impressive butler, comes in, followed by Gann. This is Claude Insoley’s gamekeeper, a short, sturdy man, grizzled, with wild stubborn hair and a fringe of beard round his chin. He wears his Sunday clothes of sombre broadcloth.
[Gann, hat in hand, advances to the middle of the room.
They’ve not got up from dinner yet, but he’ll come and see you at once.
He said I was to tell him the moment you come. What can he be wanting of you at this time of night?
Maybe if he wished you to know he’d have told you.
I don’t want to know what don’t concern me.
Pity there ain’t more like you.
Didn’t he say you was to tell him the moment I come?
I’ve only just took in the dessert. Give ’em a minute to sample the peaches.
I thought them was your orders.
You’re a nice civil-spoken one, you are.

[With an effort Gann prevents himself from replying. It is as much as he can do to keep his hands off the sleek, obsequious butler. Moore after a glance at him goes out. The gamekeeper begins to walk up and down the room like a caged beast. In a moment he hears a sound and stops still. He turns his hat round and round in his hands.
[Claude Insoley comes in. He is a man of thirty-five, rather dried-up, rather precise, neither good-looking nor plain, with a slightly dogmatic, authoritative manner.
[Claude hesitates for a moment; to conceal a slight embarrassment he lights a cigarette. Gann watches him steadily.
I suppose you know what I’ve sent for you about.
I should have thought you might guess without hurting yourself. The Rector tells me that your daughter Peggy came back last night.
I don’t know what you mean, sir.
Oh, that’s all rot, Gann. You know perfectly well what I mean. It’s a beastly matter for both of us, but it’s no good funking it.... You’ve been on the estate pretty well all your life, haven’t you?
It’s fifty-four years come next Michaelmas that my father was took on, and I was earning wages here before you was born.
My governor always said you were the best keeper he ever struck, and hang it all, I haven’t had anything to complain about either.
Anyhow, we shan’t make it any better by beating about the bush. It appears that Peggy has got into trouble in London.... I’m awfully sorry for you, and all that sort of thing.
Poor child. She’s not to blame.
[Claude gives a slight shrug of the shoulders.
I want ’er to forget all she’s gone through. It was a mistake she ever went to London, but she would go. Now I’ll keep ’er beside me. She’ll never leave me again till I’m put underground.
That’s all very fine and large, but I’m afraid Peggy can’t stay on here, Gann.
You know the rule of the estate as well as I do. When a girl gets into a mess she has to go.
You never thought so before, and this isn’t the first time you’ve seen it applied, by a long chalk.
The girl went away once and come to grief. She wellnigh killed herself with the shame of it. I’m not going to let ’er out of my sight again.
I’m afraid I can’t make an exception in your favour, Gann.
Oh, I expect she’ll be able to get a job somewhere. Mrs. Insoley’ll do all she can.
It’s no good, Squire. I can’t let ’er go. I want ’er.
I don’t want to be unreasonable. I’ll give you a certain amount of time to make arrangements.
Time’s no good to me. I haven’t the ’eart to send her away.
I’m afraid it’s not a question of whether you like it or not. You must do as you’re told.
I can’t part with her, and there’s an end of it.
You’d better go and talk it over with your wife.
I don’t want to talk it over with anyone. I’ve made up my mind.
[Claude is silent for a moment. He looks at Gann thoughtfully.
[Deliberately.] I’ll give you twenty-four hours to think about it.
[Startled.] What d’you mean by that, sir?
If Peggy isn’t gone by that time, I am afraid I shall have to send you away.
You wouldn’t do that, sir? You couldn’t do it, Squire, not after all these years.
We’ll soon see about that, my friend.
You can’t dismiss me for that. I’ll have the law of you. I’ll sue you for wrongful dismissal.
You can do what you damned well like; but if Peggy hasn’t gone by to-morrow night I shall turn you off the estate on Tuesday.
[Hoarsely.] You wouldn’t do it! You couldn’t do it.
[There is a sound of talking and laughter, and of a general movement as the dining-room door is opened.
They’re just coming in. You’d better hook it.

[Miss Vernon and Edith Lewis come in, followed by Grace. For a moment Gann stands awkwardly, and then leaves the room. Miss Vernon is a slight, faded, rather gaunt woman of thirty-five. Her deliberate manner, her composure, suggest a woman of means and a woman who knows her own mind. Edith Lewis is a pretty girl of twenty. Grace is thirty. She is a beautiful creature with an eager, earnest face and fine eyes. She has a restless manner, and her frequent laughter strikes you as forced. She is always falling from one emotion to another. She uses a slightly satirical note when she speaks to her husband.
[Going to the window.] Oh, what a lovely night! Do let’s go out. [To Grace.] May we?
Of course, if you want to.
I’m perfectly sick with envy every time I look out of the window. Those lovely old trees!
I wonder if you’d be sick with envy if you looked at nothing else for forty-six weeks in the year?
People who habitually live in London generally do.
Aren’t you fond of the country?
[Vehemently.] I hate it! I hate it with all my heart and soul.
My dear Grace, what are you saying?
It bores me. It bores me stiff. Those endless trees, and those dreary meadows, and those ploughed fields. Oh!
I don’t think I could ever get tired of the view from your dining-room.

Not if you saw it for three meals a day for ten years? Oh, my dear, you don’t know what that view is like at an early breakfast on a winter’s morning. You sit there looking at it, with icy fingers, wondering if your nose is red, while your husband reads morning prayers, because his father read morning prayers before him; and the sky looks as if it were going to sink down and crush you.
You can’t expect sunshine all the year round, can you?
Well, I’m a Cockney, and I feel inclined to fall down on my very knees and worship those big trees in your park. Oh, what a night!

lg.l: In such a night as this,
When the sweet wind did gently kiss the trees
And they did make no noise....

div.p: [Miss Vernon and Edith Lewis go out. Grace is left alone with her husband.
What on earth was Gann doing here?
I had something to say to him.
That wouldn’t be a new experience.
I say, you’re looking jolly to-night, darling.
It’s kind of you to say so.
Were you pleased with the necklace I gave you this morning?
[Smiling.] Surely I said so at the time.
I was rather hoping you’d wear it to-night.
It wouldn’t have gone with my frock.
You might have put it on all the same.
You see, your example hasn’t been lost on me. I’ve learnt to put propriety before sentiment.
[Rather shyly.] I should have thought, if you cared for me, you wouldn’t have minded.
Hang it all, I can’t help wishing sometimes you’d seem as if—you were fond of me, don’t you know.
If you’ll point out anything you particularly object to in my behaviour, I’ll try to change it.
My dear, I don’t want much, do I?
I don’t know why you should choose this particular time to make a scene.
Hang it all, I’m not making a scene!
I beg your pardon, I forgot that only women make scenes.
I only wanted to tell you that I’m just about as fond of you as I can stick.
[Suddenly touched.] After ten years of holy matrimony?
It seems about ten days to me.
Good God, to me it seems a lifetime.
I say, Grace, what d’you mean by that?
[Recovering herself.] Oughtn’t you to go back to the dining-room? Your brother and Mr. Cobbett will be boring one another.

[Claude looks at her for a moment, then rises and goes out. Grace clenches her hands, and an expression of utter wretchedness crosses her face. She passes her hand across her eyes with an impatient gesture, as if she were trying to shake herself free from some torturing thought. Moore comes in with coffee on a salver.
Put it down on the table.
Miss Vernon’s in the garden with Miss Lewis. Will you tell them that coffee is here?
[He goes out of one of the French windows into the garden. In a moment Miss Vernon comes in.
I sent her to get a wrap. We want to go down to the lake.
Thank you.... I was trying to remember how long it is since I was here last.
[Pouring out the coffee.] It was before I was married.
I’m devoted to Kenyon, I’m so glad you asked me to come and spend Whitsun here.
My mother-in-law wrote and told us that you weren’t engaged.
[With a smile.] That sounds rather chilly.
[Looking up, faintly surprised.] Certainly. If you wish it.
[Miss Vernon gives a slight smile of amusement, then gets up and stands before the fire-place with her hands behind her back.
I wonder why you dislike me so much?
I don’t know why you should think I do.
You don’t take much trouble to hide it, do you?
I’m sorry. In future I’ll be more careful.
[Rather wistfully.] I wanted to be great friends with you.
I’m afraid I don’t make friends very easily.
We live so near one another. It seems rather silly that we should only just be on speaking terms.
They wanted Claude to marry you, didn’t they? And he married me instead.
When I saw you at your wedding, I couldn’t help feeling I’d have done just the same in his place.
[With a twinkle in her eye.] And now they want you to marry his brother Archibald.
Five thousand acres in a ring fence. It seems a pity to let it go out of the family.
It’s such a nuisance that a plainish woman of six-and-thirty has to be taken along with it.
Did you ever care for Claude?
If I did or not, I’m very anxious to care for his wife.
Well, partly because I’m afraid you’re not very happy.

[Startled.] I? [Almost defiantly.] I should have thought I had everything that a woman can want to make her happy. I’ve got a husband who adores me. We’re rich. We’re—[with a sudden break in her voice]—happy! I wish to God he had married you! It’s clear enough now that he made a mistake.
[With a chuckle.] I don’t think it’s occurred to him, you know.
How many times d’you suppose his mother has said to Claude: Things would be very different now if you’d had the sense to marry Helen Vernon.
Yes, in that case I must say it’s not to be wondered at if you don’t like me very much.
Like you! I hate you with all my heart and soul!
Good gracious me, you don’t say so?
[With a sudden flash of humour.] You don’t mind my telling you, do you?
Not a bit, but I should very much like to know why?
Because I’ve got an envious disposition and I envy you.
A solitary old maid like me?

You’ve got everything that I haven’t got. D’you suppose I’ve lived ten years in my husband’s family without realising the gulf that separates Miss Vernon of Foley from the very middle-class young woman that Claude Insoley was such a damned fool as to marry? You’ve got money and I haven’t a farthing.

Oh, don’t talk such nonsense! How would you like to be dependent on somebody else for every penny you had? If I want to get Claude a Christmas present I have to buy it out of his money.... It wouldn’t be so maddening if I only had forty pounds a year of my own, but I haven’t a penny, not a penny! And I have to keep accounts. After all, it’s his money. If he wants accounts why shouldn’t he have them? I have to write down the cost of every packet of hair-pins. [With a sudden chuckle.] And the worst of it is, I never could add.
That, of course, must increase the difficulty of keeping accounts.

I’ve been an utter failure from the beginning. They despised me because I was a nobody and not even a rich nobody; but I was a strapping, healthy sort of young woman and they consoled themselves by thinking I’d have children—a milch cow was what they wanted—and I haven’t even had children....
[Miss Vernon, not knowing what to say, makes a little gesture of perplexity and helplessness. There is a brief pause.
Oh! I’m about fed up with all the humiliations I’ve had to endure.
[Edith Lewis comes in with a wrap which she gives to Miss Vernon.
Thanks so much. You’re a perfect angel.
You mustn’t stay out more than a few minutes. The men will be here in a moment, and I want to play poker. When my mother-in-law comes we shall have to mind our p’s and q’s.
Nonsense! She’s very fond of you indeed.
I could wish she had some pleasanter way of showing it than finding fault with everything I do, everything I say, and everything I wear.

Yes. [With a quizzical smile.] She’ll thoroughly disapprove of you. When I introduce you to her: This is Miss Lewis—she’ll look at you for a moment as if you were a kitchen-maid applying for a situation and say: Lewis.
Because, like myself, you’re not county.

It’s all very fine to say: Oh! but you don’t know what that means. In London, if you’re pretty and amusing and don’t give yourself airs, people are quite ready to be nice to you; but in a place like this, you can have every virtue under the sun, and if you’re not county you’re of no importance in this world, and you’ll certainly be very uncomfortable in the next.
[Smiling.] I think you’re extremely hard on us. If you have the advantage of....
[Seizing the opportunity which Miss Vernon’s hesitation gives her.] Middle-class origins?

You needn’t grudge us the perfectly harmless delusion that there is a difference between a family that has lived in the same place for three or four centuries, with traditions of good breeding and service to the country—and one that has no roots in the soil.
I seem to hear Claude’s very words.
[Good-humouredly.] Of course we have our faults.
You’re the first member of your class that I’ve ever heard acknowledge it.
[Meditatively.] I wonder if you’d despise us so much if you had a string of drunken, fox-hunting squires behind you.

Oh, my dear, when I was first married I used to lie awake at night wishing for them with all my heart. When the neighbours came to call on me I could see them obviously lying in wait for the aitches they were expecting me to drop. A Miss Robinson, wasn’t she? Robinson! Are there people called Robinson? Oh, how I wanted to scratch their ugly old faces!
How lucky I was abroad for so long! You might have disfigured me for life.
I’ve often thought that if the Archangel Gabriel came down in Somersetshire, they’d look him out in the “Landed Gentry” before they asked him to a shooting-party.
I don’t think you ought to judge us all on Mrs. Insoley. She’s a type that’s dying out.
I don’t want to seem inquisitive, but if you don’t like Mrs. Insoley why on earth d’you have her to stay here?

Simple-minded child! Because even in a county family money’s the only thing in the world that really matters, and we’re penniless, while Mrs. Insoley—[with a quick, defiant look at Miss Vernon]—Mrs. Insoley stinks of it.... Do I shock you?
[With a smile.] No, because I see you’re trying to.
Claude has nothing but the house and land and his principles. And if we’re able to have the hounds and the shooting and a couple of cars, it’s because Mrs. Insoley pays for it.
[Explaining to Edith Lewis.] Mrs. Insoley was an heiress.
She was a Bainbridge, and you’ll hear her thank God for it frequently.

[Archibald Insoley and Henry Cobbett come in. Archibald is a pleasant, good-looking man of thirty-four, with a humorous way about him, and a kindly expression. He holds the family living of Kenyon-Fulton, but there is nothing in him of the sanctimoniousness of the cloth. Cobbett is an agreeable youth of four-and-twenty. They are followed by Claude Insoley.
[Seeing Edith Lewis at the window.] Are you going out?
I’ve been preparing Miss Lewis for your mother’s arrival.
I’m beginning to tremble in my shoes.

Our mother is what is usually described as a woman of character. With the best intentions in the world and the highest principles she succeeds in making life almost intolerable to every one connected with her.
You won’t forget to send the carriage for her to-morrow, Grace?
I won’t.... Last time we sent the car by mistake, and she sent it back again.
Good heavens, why did she do that?
Mrs. Insoley never has driven in a motor-car, and Mrs. Insoley never will drive in a motor-car.
[Not unamiably.] I don’t think you ought to make fun of my mother, Grace.
I wouldn’t if I could make anything else of her.
[As she says this she sits down at the piano and rattles her fingers over the keys.
Will you sing us a song, Mr. Cobbett?
I’m afraid I don’t know anything that will fit the occasion.
I seem to have heard you warble a graceful little ditty about a top note.
Thank you very much, but I’m not fond of making a fool of myself.
Part of a gentleman’s education should be how to make himself ridiculous with dignity.
[To Cobbett.] You make more fuss about singing than a young lady at a tea-party.
[Looking at him with smiling lips but with hard eyes.] Let us have no more maidenly coyness.

[She begins to play, and Cobbett, shrugging his shoulders, begins with rather bad grace to sing the song, “I can’t reach that top note.” While they are in the middle of it the door opens, and the Butler announces Mrs. Insoley and her companion. Mrs. Insoley is a little old lady of some corpulence, shabbily dressed in rusty black. She looks rather like a charwoman in her Sunday best. Miss Hall, her companion, is a self-effacing silent person of uncertain age. She is always very anxious to make herself useful.

[The singing abruptly ceases. There is general consternation. Mrs. Insoley stops still for one moment, and surveys the party with indignation. Then she sweeps into the room with such majesty as is compatible with her small size and considerable obesity.
Is this a lunatic asylum that I have come into?
We didn’t expect you till to-morrow.
So I imagined by the fact that I found no conveyance at the station. I had to take a fly, and it cost me four-and-sixpence.
But why didn’t you let us know you’d changed your plans, mother?
I did let you know. I wrote to Grace yesterday. She must have got my letter this morning.
Oh, how stupid of me! I recognised your writing, and as it was my birthday I thought I wouldn’t open it till to-morrow.
It was only by the mercy of Providence that I didn’t have to walk.
There are always flies at the station.
Providence might very well have caused them to be all engaged.
I don’t know why you should think Providence has nothing better to do than to play practical jokes on us.
[Looking round.] And may I inquire why you have turned the house in which your father died into a bear garden?
It’s Grace’s birthday, and we thought there would be no harm in our having a little fun.
[Putting up her face-à-main and staring at the company.] I’m old-fashioned enough and well-bred enough to like people to be introduced to me.
Nowadays every one’s so disreputable that we think it safer not to make introductions.... This is Miss Lewis.
[With a little smile of amusement.] I think you know Miss Vernon of Foley.
[Very affably.] Of course I know Miss Vernon of Foley. My dear Helen, you’re looking very handsome. It wants a woman of birth to wear the outrageous costumes of the present day.
[Shaking hands with her.] It’s so nice of you to say so.
I forget if you know Mr. Cobbett.
[He bows slightly as Mrs. Insoley looks at him through her glasses.
[Turning to Miss Hall.] We used to have a milkman called Cobbett, Louisa.
Our milkman is called Wilkinson now.
[Very graciously.] You were singing a song when I came in. What was it called?
[Rather sulkily.] “I can’t reach that top note.”
I wondered why you were trying.... Why are you hiding behind that sofa, Archibald? Do you not intend to kiss your mother?
I’m delighted to see you, my dear mother.
I’m rather surprised to see a clergyman at a dinner-party on a Sunday night.
I find two sermons a day excellent for the appetite. And the Bible tells us that corn makes the young men cheerful.
[Smiling.] Aren’t you dreadfully hungry? Wouldn’t you like something to eat?
No, I shall go straight to my room. It always upsets me to drive in a hired carriage.
I’ll just go and see that everything’s nice and comfortable.
Pray don’t put yourself to any trouble on my account. It would distress me.
[Aside to Miss Vernon.] Don’t you think we might go down to the lake?
By all means.... There’s nothing I can get you, Mrs. Insoley?
[Miss Vernon and Edith Lewis go out, and a moment later Cobbett slips out also.
Claude, will you take Miss Hall into the dining-room and give her a sandwich and a glass of port?
I don’t think I want anything, thank you, Mrs. Insoley.
Nonsense, Louisa! Allow me to know what is good for you. You’ll see that she drinks the port, Claude. [As they go out.] I want to talk to Archibald.
My dear mother, I throw myself at your feet.
[With a chuckle.] I very much doubt if you could. You’re growing much too fat. It’s quite time they made you something.
[Smiling.] The landed gentry hasn’t its old power. Promotion in the Church nowadays is given with new-fangled ideas about merit and scholarship and heaven knows what.
I hope you never eat potatoes or bread?
I fly from them as I would from temptation.
It is as the scarlet woman to me.
And I trust you never touch green peas.
Ah, there you have me. Even the saints had their weaknesses. I confess that when green peas are in season I always put on flesh.
You want some one to keep a firm hand on you. You must marry.
I saw you approaching that topic by leaps and bounds, mother.
It’s a clergyman’s duty to marry.
[Interrupting.] I know what St. Paul’s views were, Archibald, and I disagree with them.
[Dryly.] I have every reason to believe he was of excellent family, mother.
[Giving him a quick look.] We all know that it was a great disappointment to Helen Vernon when—you know what I mean.
I can’t help thinking she showed bad taste in surviving the blow.
It was a great disappointment to me. I had set my heart on joining Foley to Kenyon-Fulton.... It wouldn’t be too late even now if you had the sense to appreciate Helen Vernon’s affection for you.
My dear mother, I can’t persuade myself for a moment that Helen Vernon has any affection for me.
A woman of her age is prepared to have affection for any one who asks her to marry him.
Even if he’s a poor country parson?
You’re a great deal more than a country parson, Archibald. It is unlikely that Grace will have any children, so unless—something happens to allow Claude to marry again....
What d’you mean by that, mother?
On the other hand, she has excellent health.
There may be other ways of disposing of her.
[Looking at him calmly.] Since when have you laboured under the delusion that I am the sort of woman to submit to cross-examination, Archibald?
[The entrance of Grace interrupts the conversation.
I hope I haven’t kept you waiting. I think you’ll find everything all right.
In that case I shall go to my room. Archibald, tell Louisa that I am ready to go to my room.
[He goes out, leaving Grace alone with Mrs. Insoley.
Who is the young lady you have staying with you, Grace?
Edith Lewis. She’s a friend of mine.
Ah! And who is this Mr. Cobbett?
He’s a friend of mine too.
I didn’t imagine that you would invite total strangers to stay with you.
I don’t know that there’s any other way of describing them.
I dare say that is a sufficient description in itself.
[Miss Hall comes back with Claude and Archibald.
I’m going to my room, Louisa. I shall be ready for you to read to me in a quarter of an hour.
Very good, Mrs. Insoley. [To Grace.] I suppose you don’t have prayers on Sunday night?
No, we read our pedigree instead. You’ll find the “Landed Gentry” in your bedroom.
[Icily.] In my young days it was thought more important for a young lady to be well-born than to be clever.
[Chuckling.] The result has been disastrous for the present generation.
[Shaking hands cordially with Miss Hall.] Be sure and let me know if you’re not quite comfortable. I hope you’ll find everything you want in your room.
Of course Louisa will find everything she wants. She wants nothing. Come, Louisa.
[Mrs. Insoley and Miss Hall go out.
I think I’ll be toddling back to my rectory.
[To Archibald.] I talked to Gann about that matter.
I’m afraid he’s going to make rather a nuisance of himself.
I took a good firm line, you know.
That’s right. It’s the only way with those sort of fellows. Good night, old man.
You were asking about Gann just now, Grace?
At first I thought I’d better not tell you anything about it, but I’ve been thinking it over....
[Interrupting.] It was quite unnecessary. I’m not at all curious.
I think perhaps it would be better if I told you what I’d done.
I’m sure that whatever you’ve done is right, Claude. [Smiling.] That’s why you’re so detestable.
That’s all very fine and large, but I think I’d like to have your approval.
We agreed very early in our married life that your acts were such as must necessarily meet with my approval.
What’s the matter with you, Grace?
You’ve been so funny lately. I haven’t been able to make you out at all.
I should have thought you had more important things to do than to bother about me.
I’ve got nothing in the world to do more important than to bother about you, Grace.
[She looks at him for an instant, with a catch in her breath.
Don’t worry me to-night, Claude; my head’s aching so that I feel I could scream.
[With the tenderest concern.] My poor child, why didn’t you tell me? I’m so sorry I’ve been bothering you. Is it very bad?
What a beast I am! How can you like me when I’m so absolutely horrid to you?
My darling, I don’t blame you for having a headache.
I’m sorry I was beastly to you just now.
[He tries to take her in his arms, but she draws herself away.
Why don’t you go to bed, darling?
[With a cry of something like fright.] Oh, no!
Bed’s the best place for everybody at this hour.
I want to amuse myself. Go and fetch the others, they’re down by the lake. And we’ll all play poker.
[He is just going to make an observation, but she bursts in vehemently.
For God’s sake do as I ask you.
[He looks at her. With a shrug of the shoulders he goes out into the garden. Grace gives a deep sigh. In a moment Henry Cobbett enters. Grace looks at him silently as he advances into the room.
I’ve been waiting for the chance of speaking to you by yourself.
Why did you make me sing that idiotic song just now?
[Her eyes cold and hostile.] Because I chose.
You made me look a perfect fool.
That’s what I wanted to make you look.
I have no explanation to offer.
You know, I’m hanged if I can make you out. You’re never the same for two minutes together.
[Frigidly.] I suppose it is disconcerting. Claude complains of it too.
You’re growing more and more like him every day, Harry.
I don’t quite know what you mean by that.
It seems hardly worth while to have—made a long journey to find oneself exactly where one started.
I never know what people are driving at when they talk metaphorically.
[Looking at him deliberately.] I thought I loved you, Harry.
[Slowly.] I wonder if I just said it to persuade myself. My heart’s empty! Empty! I know now that it wasn’t love I felt for you.
It’s rather late in the day to have found that out, isn’t it?
[Bitterly.] Yes, that’s just it. It’s late in the day for everything.... Here they are.
[A sound of talking is heard as Edith Lewis approaches with Helen Vernon and Claude.
[At the window.] I found them on their way back.
[To Cobbett, with a little bitter laugh.] We’re going to play poker.

div.head: THE SECOND ACT
div.p: The Scene is the same as in the preceding Act. It is evening, towards seven o’clock, but it is still perfectly light. Grace and Peggy Gann are in the room, both standing. Peggy is a pretty girl, quite young, but very pale, with black rings round her eyes. She is dressed like a housemaid in her going-out things. Grace is evidently much distressed.
You will try, mum, won’t you?
[Peggy’s voice seems to call Grace back with a start from her own thoughts.
I ought to have been told before. It was wicked to keep it from me.
I thought you knew, mum. I wasn’t to know that you ’adn’t been told anything.
[With a friendly smile.] I’m not blaming you, Peggy.... Mr. Insoley’s out now, but I’ll talk to him as soon as she come in. You’d better go home and fetch your father.
You know what father is, mum. I’m afraid he won’t come.
Oh, but I think it’s very important. Tell him that....
[Henry Cobbett comes in, and she stops when she sees him.
Hulloa, am I in the way? Shall I go?
[Passing her hand wearily across her forehead.] No. I’ve just finished.... Try and get your father to come, Peggy.
Well, I’ll do what I can, mum.
[She goes out. Grace gives a little exclamation, partly of distress, partly of indignation.
What’s the matter? You seem rather put out.

That’s the daughter of one of the keepers. She came to me just now and asked me to beg Claude to give them a little more time. I hadn’t an idea what she meant. Then she said Claude had told her father he must send her away within twenty-four hours or lose his place.
[Flippantly.] Oh, yes, I know. She seems to be rather a flighty young person. Claude and your brother-in-law were talking about it after lunch in the smoking-room.
Well, it never struck me you didn’t know. Besides—you haven’t shown any great desire for my society the last day or two.
[With a quick look at him.] I’ve had other guests to attend to.
[Shrugging his shoulders.] And it seemed rather a sordid little story. I don’t think I can interest myself very much at this time of day in the gamekeeper’s daughter who kicks over the traces.
[Sarcastically.] It’s so devilish mid-Victorian, isn’t it?
[Surprised at her tone.] It’s not really bothering you, is it?
[With a sudden vehement outburst.] Don’t you see that wretched girl has done no more than I have?
[With a chuckle.] Great Scott, you haven’t produced an unexpected baby, have you?
[Coolly.] In point of fact she’s done a great deal more than you have. She’s been found out.
How can you be so odiously cynical?
I notice people always call you odiously cynical when you talk plain horse-sense to them.
Can’t you realise what I’m feeling? She had excuses. She was alone, and little more than a child; she had no education. How could she be expected to resist temptation?

It’s an absolute delusion that the lower classes are less able to resist temptation than their betters. In the first place, they have a much more systematic moral education, and then they’re taught from early youth to look upon virtue as a valuable asset.
[Going up to him suddenly.] Harry, would you mind very much if I stopped the whole thing?
Oh, no, don’t say that because it’s the conventional thing to say. I want you to be frank with me.
[Uneasily.] Why do you ask me now?
[After a look at him, a little unwillingly.] I feel so horribly mean.

[With a sort of appeal, as if she were excusing herself.] He’s so awfully good to me, Harry. Every present he gives me, every kind word is like a stab in my heart. I’m beastly to him sometimes, I can’t help it, but nothing seems to make any difference to him.... Whatever I do, he loves me.
Are you beginning to care for Claude—differently?
Oh, it’s no use pretending. I never loved him as he loved me. I couldn’t. I was bored by his love. Yes, all the time we’ve been married.... It’s only lately....
[She pauses abruptly. Cobbett gives her a sidelong glance.

I don’t know what I feel or what to do. I’m so bewildered and wretched.... He bores me still—oh, horribly sometimes. And yet at moments I feel as though I were a good deal more than half in love with him. It’s too absurd. With Claude—after all these years. Something has changed me.... It’s the last thing that ought to have changed me towards him.
[She flushes hotly, and again Cobbett looks at her, and a rather sulky expression comes into his face.
It’s not a very pleasant position for me, is it?
I shouldn’t have thought it ever had been a very pleasant position considering what a good friend Claude has been to you.
If you look at it in that way, I dare say it would be better to put an end to the whole thing.
You have been rather a blackguard, haven’t you?

No. I don’t pretend to be better than anybody else, but I’m quite certain I’m no worse. I’m a perfectly normal man in good health. It’s idiotic to abuse me because I’ve done what any other fellow would have done in my place.
[Suddenly understanding.] Is that all it was to you?

Wasn’t I anything to you at all? Only a more or less attractive woman who happened to cross your path? If I was only that, why couldn’t you leave me alone? What harm did I ever do you? Oh, it was cruel of you. Cruel!
[Quietly.] No man’s able to have an affair all by himself, you know.
Well, most fellows are very shy, and they’re dreadfully frightened of a rebuff. A man doesn’t take much risk until—well, until he finds there’s not much risk to take.
D’you mean to say I gave you to understand.... Oh, how can you humiliate me like that?
Isn’t there a certain amount of truth in it?
[Looking as it were into her own soul.] Yes.... Oh, I’m so ashamed.
The world would be a jolly sight easier place to live in if people weren’t such humbugs.
[Hardly able to believe the truth that presents itself to her, yet eager to probe it.] D’you think it was only curiosity on my side and nothing more than opportunity on yours?
That’s the foundation of nine love affairs out of ten, you know.

[Trying to justify herself in her own eyes.] I was so bored—so lonely. I never felt at home with the people I had to live with. They humiliated me. And you seemed the same sort of person as I was. I felt at my ease with you. At first I thought you cared for the things I cared for—music and books and pictures: it took me quite a time to discover that you didn’t know the difference between a fiddle and a jews’ harp.... I wonder why you troubled to take me in.
I naturally talked about what I thought would please you.

I remember at first I felt as if I were just stepping out of a prison into the fresh air. It seemed to me as if—oh, I don’t know how to put it—as if spring flowers were suddenly blossoming in my heart.
I’m afraid you were asking more from me than I was able to give you.

Oh, I don’t blame you. You’re quite right: it’s I who am to blame. [With sudden vehemence.] Oh, how I envy that wretched girl! If she fell it was because she loved. I asked her who the man was, and she wouldn’t tell me. She said she didn’t want to get him into trouble. She must love him still.
[Moved by the pain which he sees she is suffering.] I hope you don’t think me an awful skunk, Grace. I’m sorry we’ve made such a hash of things.
[Going on with her own thoughts.] It would be horrible if that wretched girl were punished while I go scot-free. I can’t let her be turned away like a leper. I should never rest in peace again.
Claude’s not very fond of going back on his word. He seems to have delivered an ultimatum, and I expect he’ll stick to it.
It means so much to me. I feel somehow that if I can only save that poor child it’ll make up in a way—oh, very little—for all the harm I’ve done.... D’you think I’m perfectly absurd?
Life seems devilish complicated sometimes, doesn’t it?
[The sound is heard of a carriage stopping outside.
It’s my mother-in-law. She’s been out for her drive. [With a glance at her watch.] Claude ought to be in soon.
What are you going to do?
I’m going to use every means in my power to persuade him to change his mind.
You’re not going to do anything foolish, Grace?
How d’you mean? [His meaning suddenly strikes her.] You don’t think I might have to.... Oh, that would be too much to ask me.... D’you think I might have to tell him?
Whatever you do, Grace, I want you to know that if anything happens I’m willing to do the straight thing.
[Shaking her head.] No, I should never ask you to marry me. Now we both know how things are between us—how they’ve always been....

There’s no need to be. I’m glad to know the truth. There was nothing that held us together before but my cowardice. I was so afraid of going back to that dreary loneliness. But you’ve given me courage.
Is there nothing left of it at all?
So far as I’m concerned nothing at all—but shame.
[Edith Lewis comes in. Grace, recovering herself quickly, throws off her seriousness and greets the girl with a pleasant smile.
We’ve had such a lovely drive.
And d’you think the country’s as beautiful as ever?

[Gaily.] Oh, I didn’t look at the country. I was much too excited. Mrs. Insoley has been telling me the dreadful pasts of all the families in the neighbourhood. It appears the further they go back the more shocking their behaviour has been.
I notice that even the grossest immorality becomes respectable when it’s a hundred years old.
[Ironically.] It’s very hard, isn’t it? Mrs. Grundy has no mercy. She’ll take even you to her bosom before you know where you are.
[Enter Mrs. Insoley, followed by Miss Vernon and Miss Hall. Miss Hall is carrying Mrs. Insoley’s lap-dog.
I hope you enjoyed your drive.
I didn’t go for my enjoyment, Grace; I went to exercise the horses.
[Smiling.] Meanwhile, I hear you took the opportunity of enlarging Edith’s young mind.
[To Edith.] When you come to Foley you must remind me to show you the portraits of my great-grandmother, Mary Vernon. She had a tremendous affair with the Regent, you know.
[Pleasantly.] My dear Helen, I have the greatest affection for you, but I cannot allow a statement like that to go unchallenged. There is no evidence whatever of the truth of it.
I don’t know how you can say that, Mrs. Insoley, considering that I have all my great-grandmother’s letters to the Regent.
[With a chuckle.] Where are his letters to your great-grandmother?
She gave them back at the time he returned hers, naturally.
I can see her. If she had any letters she would have kept them. Any woman would.
[Bridling a little.] I can’t imagine why you should suddenly throw doubts on a story that the whole county has believed for a hundred years. Every one knew all about Mary Vernon.
[Chaffing her.] I am aware that your great-grandmother was an abandoned hussy, but that in itself is no proof that she ever had anything to do with the Regent.
You can’t deny that he slept at Foley, Mrs. Insoley.

It’s notorious that at that very time he was on terms of the greatest intimacy with Pamela Bainbridge. [To Edith Lewis.] I am not an Insoley, thank God; I am a Bainbridge. And whenever he came to this part of the country he stayed with us.
I know you’ve always flattered yourself that there was something between them.
[With complete self-assurance.] And well I may, considering that I still have a lock of hair which he gave my grandmother.
Half the families in the country have a greasy lock of hair which they tell you was the Regent’s. Personally, I think it’s rather snobbish to make a claim of that sort unless one’s perfectly sure.
[Bridling in her turn.] I think you’re extremely rude, Helen. In the presence of a man I can’t go into details, but I have proof of every word I say. You know what I mean, Louisa?
I believed the worst from the beginning, Mrs. Insoley.
I have no doubt you firmly believe what you say, Mrs. Insoley; but if you don’t mind my saying so, one has only to look at the portrait of Pamela Bainbridge to know the whole thing’s absurd.
[Frigidly.] We won’t argue the point, Helen; I know I’m right, and there’s an end of it.... Put the dog on that chair, Louisa.
That’s Mr. Cobbett’s chair, Mrs. Insoley.
[Still a little out of temper.] Has Mr. Cobbett bought it?
No, but Mr. Cobbett’s been sitting in it.
And may no one use a chair that Mr. Cobbett has been sitting in?
Certainly. But it so happens that Mr. Cobbett is just going to sit in it again.
[With a grim smile.] Mr. Cobbett has legs.
Only two, and if a merciful Providence had intended him to stand on them it would undoubtedly have provided him with four.
Mr. Cobbett seems to be better acquainted with the designs of Providence than I should have expected.... Louisa, give me the dog. He shall sit on my lap.
[Chaffing her.] Ah, if you’d only told me that was the alternative, of course I wouldn’t have hesitated for a moment.
I think you are very vulgar, sir.... I’m surprised that you should laugh at such an inane joke, Grace.
You forget that I have a naturally vulgar nature.
I try to, but you take great pains to remind me.
Well, did you enjoy your drive, mother?
I didn’t go for my enjoyment, Claude; I went to exercise the horses.
We’ve been to a parish meeting.
[Rather peevishly.] It’s getting almost impossible to do anything for these Somersetshire people. They’re such an obstinate, pig-headed lot.
I prophesied it forty years ago. When they first introduced all this nonsense about education, I said it was a serious matter.
[With a twinkle in his eye.] Like all good prophets you apparently took care to be rather vague about it, mother.

Considering you weren’t born I don’t see what you can know about it, Archibald. I said this would happen. I said they would make the lower classes so independent that no one would be able to do anything with them. I went for a walk in the village this morning and nobody took any notice of me. Isn’t that so, Louisa?
What do you mean by no, Louisa?
[Hastily.] I beg your pardon. I mean yes, Mrs. Insoley.
A few old men touched their hats, and one old woman curtsied, but that was all.
[With a little nod.] Of course it’s not important in itself, but it’s the sign of a change. The long and short of it is that they don’t look up to their betters as they used to.
[Ironically.] Perhaps they’ve ceased to realise that we are their betters.
It’s not too late to teach them their mistake. Personally I mean to be master in my own house.
[Abruptly.] Peggy Gann came to see me this afternoon, Claude.
[There is a very short pause. Cobbett sees what is going to happen and gets up.
[To Edith Lewis.] Wouldn’t you like to come for a stroll in the garden?
I’ve asked her to fetch her father.
[Without waiting for the movement.] I’m sorry you did that, Grace. I’ve got nothing to say to him.
[To Mrs. Insoley.] Do you know that Claude has threatened to dismiss Gann if Peggy hasn’t gone by ten o’clock to-night?
For once in his life Claude has acted with spirit. He gave Gann twenty-four hours to think it over. My father would have given him fifteen minutes.
Why was it all kept from me? It seems that everybody knew but me.
Hang it all, Grace, I wanted to tell you last night and you wouldn’t let me.
[Startled.] Oh! Was it that? I didn’t know.... Claude, I want you to be very kind and forgive that wretched girl. I want you to tell Gann that she needn’t go.
[Quite firmly.] My dear, I can’t do that. I’ve made up my mind and I must stick to it.

Hang it all, what would happen to the discipline of the estate if I were always shilly-shallying? Every one in the place knows that when I say a thing I mean it. It’s an enormous advantage to all concerned.
[With a coaxing smile.] It wouldn’t do any harm if you made an exception just this once.
It’s a matter of upholding my authority. Gann refused to do what I told him, and I had to threaten him with immediate dismissal. I couldn’t eat my words now without looking a perfect fool.
Don’t you think it’s awfully unjust to send a girl away because she’s got into trouble?
It’s a rule of the estate. I didn’t make it.
[Turning to Miss Vernon.] Helen, you’re a woman. You must see how cruel it is. Can’t you say something to help me?
I don’t know what else one’s to do. After all, we have the same rule at Foley.
They have it on half the large estates in the kingdom. It’s absolutely essential if one has any regard for decency.
I don’t suppose it would be so common, and it certainly wouldn’t have lasted so long, if there hadn’t been some good in it.

[Violently.] Oh, it’s maddening. Always, always, there’s that stone wall in front of me. Whatever is, is good. However cruel and unjust a custom is, no one must touch it because it’s a custom. If a law is infamous, does it become any less infamous because people have suffered from it for a dozen generations?
Perhaps you’re not very competent to judge matters of this sort, my dear.
I’m afraid your sympathy is rather wasted in this particular case. Peggy Gann isn’t a very deserving young woman.
If she were, there’d be no need for me to plead for her.
On those lines the more of a hussy a girl is the more she’s deserving of sympathy.
[To Archibald.] You had nothing against her till this happened.
Nothing very definite. She was always rather cheeky, and she never came to Sunday-school very regularly.
My own belief is that the Ganns are really Dissenters.
[Impatiently.] Good heavens, they positively revel in going to church.
That may be or it may not. But they give me the impression of chapel people.
Heaven knows, I don’t want to seem hard and unsympathetic, but after all, you’re not going to keep people moral if you pamper those who aren’t.
And what d’you think’ll happen to her if you make her leave here?
We’ll do our best for her. It’s not a pleasant position for any of us, Grace. I’ve been wretched about the whole thing, and I’m sure Claude has too.

Of course I have. But hang it all, in our position we can’t afford to think of sentiment. Especially now that they’re attacking us all round we’ve got to show them that we can keep a firm hand on the reins.

Do us the justice to see that we’re really trying to do what’s right. It may be very wrong that we should be in our particular positions, and we may be quite unworthy of them. But we didn’t make society, and we’re not responsible for its inequalities. We find ourselves in a certain station, and we have to act accordingly.
The long and the short of it is that it’s our duty to look after those whom Providence has placed in our charge. And it’s our duty to punish as well as to reward.

Oh, how hard you are! One would think you’d never done anything in your life that you regret. [With increasing violence.] Oh, you virtuous people, I hate you. You’re never content till you see the sinner actually frizzling. As if hell were needed when every sin brings its own punishment! And you never make excuses. You don’t know how many temptations we resist for the one we fall to.

[Grace, almost beside herself, looks at her with haggard eyes. Suddenly she gives a start, and stares at Miss Vernon with horror. She has realised that Miss Vernon knows the relations that have existed between her and Henry Cobbett. There is a pause. The Butler comes in.
Gann and his daughter are here, sir.
Oh, yes, I’ll come at once.
Why shouldn’t he come here, Claude?
Yes, let him come by all means. And then you can see for yourselves.
I’ll tell Moore, shall I? [He goes to the door as he says this and calls.] Moore. Tell Gann to come here.
[Rising.] I think I’ll leave you. This isn’t any business of mine. [To Miss Hall.] Will you come with me?
Do you want me, Mrs. Insoley?
No. You’ve had no exercise to-day, Louisa. You’d better walk three times round the garden.
I’m not very well to-day, Mrs. Insoley.
Oh, nonsense! You’re in the best of health. And you can take the dog with you.
[Miss Vernon and Miss Hall go out.
Louisa’s very troublesome sometimes. She fancies she’s not feeling well. But she’s twenty-five years younger than I am, and I’ve never had a day’s illness in my life.
[Moore opens the door for Gann, who comes into the room, cap in hand, and stands at the door awkwardly. He is in his working clothes.
Good afternoon, sir. Peggy said you wished to see me, sir.
I asked her to bring you here, Gann. I thought it would be better if you spoke to Mr. Insoley.
I’ve got nothing to say to Mr. Insoley, ma’am.
I was hoping to find you in a more reasonable state of mind, Gann. You know, you can only hurt yourself by being pig-headed and stubborn.
I didn’t know as how I was, sir.
[To Grace.] You see, the man doesn’t give me a chance.
[Making an effort on himself.] Please, Squire, I come to know if I’m really to go to-morrow? I know you said you’d send me away, Squire. But I couldn’t bring myself to believe you meant it.
I’m willing to listen to anything you’ve got to say. I want to be quite fair to you.
If I could only make you see as what you ask ain’t possible, I’m sure you’d let us stay. There’s nowhere Peggy can go to.
Hang it all, Mrs. Insoley’ll do all she can for her. You may be quite sure that Peggy shan’t want for money.
It isn’t money the girl wants. If I send ’er away she’ll just go to the bad altogether.
You see, it’s a matter of principle, Gann. It would be devilish unjust to make an exception in your favour.
[Stepping forward with surly indignation and facing Claude.] I love the girl and I can’t bear to part with ’er. She’s a good girl in her ’eart, only she’s had a misfortune.
That’s all very fine and large, Gann. But if she’d been a good girl, hang it all, she’d have had power to resist temptation.
[Terrified.] Claude, you don’t know what you’re saying.

I don’t want to rub it in and all that sort of thing, but my own feeling is that if she came rather a cropper, it was because she was—if you don’t mind my saying so—because she was that way inclined. I don’t think anyone can accuse me of being a hard man, but I’m afraid I haven’t much pity for women who....
[Interrupting.] Claude, don’t go on—for God’s sake.
That’s your last word, Squire? If the girl don’t go, I must?

I’ve served you faithful, man and boy, for forty years. And I was born in that there cottage I live in now. If you turn us out where are we to go to? I’m getting on in years, and I shan’t find it easy to get another job. It’ll mean the work’us.
I’m very sorry. I can’t do anything for you. You’ve had your chance and you’ve refused to take it.
[Gann turns his cap round nervously. His face is distorted with agony. He opens his mouth to speak, but no words come, only an inarticulate groan. He turns on his heel.
In consideration of your long service I’ll give you fifty pounds so that you can tide over the next few months.
[Violently.] You can keep your dirty money.
[He goes out. Grace goes up to Claude desperately.
Oh, Claude, you can’t do it. You’ll break the man’s heart. Haven’t you any pity? Haven’t you any forgiveness?
It’s no good, Grace. I must stick to what I’ve said.
It’s not often I’ve begged you to do anything for me.
Well, hang it all, this is the first time I’ve ever refused.
[Bitterly.] I suppose because I’ve never asked you for anything before that wasn’t absolutely trifling.
Why are you making such a point of it, Grace?
Is it very strange that I should feel sorry for anyone who’s in distress?
I’ll do anything in the world to please you, darling, but in this case you must trust to my better judgment.
How can you be so hard?
Come, Grace, don’t be angry with me. It’s bad enough as it is.
I have no patience with you, Claude. When your father made up his mind to do anything it was done, and it would never have occurred to me to oppose him.
[With a twinkle in his eye.] You forget, mother, that was because you generally made up my father’s mind some time before he did.
[To Mrs. Insoley and Archibald.] Will you leave me alone with Claude. I must talk to him alone.
Come, mother. Let me take you for a stroll three times round the garden.

I couldn’t say it before them. They’d never understand. They’d only sneer. But can’t you see, Claude, that it’s out of the question to drive Gann away so callously? He loves the place just as much as you love it.... In my heart I seem to feel suddenly all that his shabby little cottage means to him—the woods and coverts and the meadows and the trees. His life is bound up with Kenyon. His roots are in the earth as if he were a growing thing. Can’t you see what it must mean to him to leave it?

He only goes because he’s headstrong and obstinate. He’s the Somersetshire peasant all over. You do your best for them and you get no gratitude. You try to reason with them, but you can’t get a single idea into their thick heads.
You can’t punish him because he’s stupid and dull. You’re throwing him upon the world in his old age. It means starvation.
You must know that I’m only doing it because I think it’s my duty.
[Impatiently.] Oh, men always talk of their duty when they want to be odiously cruel.
Grace, how can you be so unkind to me?

Oh, Claude, if you love me at all, give in to me this time. You don’t know what it means to me. I’ve often been horrible to you, but I’m going to be different. I want to love you. I want to be more to you than I’ve ever been. Claude, I implore you to do what I ask you—just because I ask it, because you love me.
[Withdrawing himself a little.] I could not love you, dear, so much, loved I not honour....

[Interrupting passionately.] Oh, no, don’t, Claude; for God’s sake be sincere and natural. Can’t you forget that you’re a landed proprietor and a J.P. and all the rest of it, and remember that you’re only a man, as weak and as—as frail as the rest of us? You hope to be forgiven yourself, and you’re utterly pitiless.
My darling, it’s just as much for your sake that I’m firm.
[Impatiently.] Oh, how can you make phrases! What on earth have I got to do with it?
Hang it all, don’t you see that it’s because of you that I can’t give way? It’s beastly having to say it. It makes me feel such an ass.
[Beginning to be frightened.] What have I got to do with it?
Until I knew you I don’t suppose I had a higher opinion of women than most men, but you taught me what a—what a stunning fine thing a good woman is.
[Hoarsely.] It’s perfectly absurd. It’s—it’s unreasonable. I’ve not been.... Only the other day you said I was cold. And just now you told me I was unkind.
I dare say that’s all my fault. I expect I bore you sometimes. After all, I know you’re worth about six of me. I can’t expect you to love me as I love you.
D’you mean to say that if I weren’t—what you think me, you wouldn’t insist on that poor girl going away?
I don’t suppose I should feel quite the same about it.
[Trying to keep back her sobs.] It’s so unreasonable.

Even if it weren’t for the rule of the estate, I couldn’t let her live in the same place as you. I can’t help it. It’s just a sort of instinct. It simply disgusts me to think that you may meet that—that woman when you walk about, and her kid.
Oh, Claude, you don’t know what you’re saying.
When I heard she’d been here and you’d been talking to her, I felt almost sick.
[Breaking down.] Oh, I can’t bear it.
Come, darling, don’t let’s quarrel any more. It hurts me so awfully.
[To herself.] Oh, I can’t. I can’t.
I?... If I weren’t what you.... Oh, it’s too much to ask anyone. Claude, I beseech you to give way.
[He shakes his head. She falls back in despair, realising that there is no way to move him.
[The sound of a gong is heard. Claude looks at his watch.
By Jove, I had no idea it was so late. There’s the dressing gong. You must hurry up.
[Looking at him vaguely.] What is it?
Time to dress for dinner, darling. You won’t be late, will you? You know how mother hates to be kept waiting.

[He takes her hand and presses it, then hurries out. She has given him her hand inertly, and it falls heavily to her side as he drops it. She remains standing where he left her. She tries to stifle the tearless sobs that seem to choke her. The Butler comes in.
Peggy Gann wishes to know if you want to see her again, madam.
[With a start.] Has she been waiting all this time?
Yes’m. She didn’t know as Gann had left. He never come back to the servants’ hall.
[He goes out. In a moment he opens the door for Peggy Gann.
Oh, Peggy, how ill you look! I’ve been able to do nothing for you.
[With a cry of distress.] Oh, mum, I was hoping. You said you’d do your best for me.
My dear, I’m so dreadfully sorry for you.
It’s so ’ard on me, mum, and so ’ard on father. Wasn’t there something more you could do, mum?
[With a little gasp of anguish.] I did all I could. I couldn’t do anything more. I couldn’t really.... [Almost to herself.] It’s too much to ask anyone.
I’ve got to go then, and there’s an end of it. You won’t let father be turned away, will you, mum? That’s all I care about now. It ’ud just break his ’eart.
[With a ray of hope.] D’you think he’ll let you go? I think it’s the best thing after all, Peggy. I’ve done—I’ve done all I could.
No, he won’t hear of it. But I shall go all the same—somewhere he can’t find me.
[Anxious now to make the best of it.] I dare say it won’t be for very long, Peggy. Have you as much money as you want? I should like to do something for you.
I shan’t want anything, thank you, mum. And thank you for all you’ve done. And if anything come to ’appen to me, you’d see as the baby wasn’t sent to the workhouse, wouldn’t you, mum?
How d’you mean? I don’t understand.
I’m not going to take the baby with me, mum. It would only be a hindrance.
[With a sigh of relief.] Oh, I was so afraid you meant....
Is there anything else you want me for, mum?
Then I’ll say good evening, mum.
[She watches Peggy go out, then she gives a little moan of despair.
There you are! I thought you were in your room. Your maid said you hadn’t come up yet.
[With a smile.] I’ve got something dreadfully important to ask you.

Well, I want to know if you’re going to wear the grey satin you wore on Saturday. You see, I only brought three dinner dresses down with me, and one of them’s a grey, only it’s much more slaty than yours, and it’ll look so cold beside it. So I shan’t put it on if you’re going to wear yours.
[Dully.] No, I won’t wear my grey satin.
What are you going to wear?
I don’t want to clash with you.
[Clenching her hands to prevent herself from screaming.] I won’t put on anything that’ll interfere with your grey.
Thank you. Now I can be quite happy. I say, we shall be so late.
[She runs off. Grace gives a little answering laugh to hers; and as Edith Lewis goes out, it lengthens into a mirthless, low, hysterical peal, broken with sobs.

div.head: THE THIRD ACT
div.p: [The dining-room at Kenyon Fulton. It is a fine room with French windows leading into the garden. On the walls are departed Insoleys of the last two or three generations, stiff ladies and gentlemen of the Victorian era, military-looking fellows in the uniform of the early nineteenth century, and ungainly Georgian squires with their wives in powdered hair. Between the windows, standing well away from the wall, rather far back, is a round table laid out for breakfast. On the Sheraton sideboard is a cloth, a stand for keeping dishes warm, a large ham, and plates and forks and spoons. Against the wall opposite the sideboard are a row of chairs, and there are half a dozen chairs round the table. There are doors right and left.

It is the morning after the events which occur in the Second Act, and when the curtain rises prayers have just finished. Claude is seated at the table with an immense prayer-book and a still larger Bible in front of him. The rest of the party are rising to their feet. They have been kneeling against various chairs. They consist of Mrs. Insoley, Miss Hall, and Miss Vernon. Well away from them, emphasising the fact that even the Almighty must recognise the difference between the gentry and their inferiors, have been praying the servants. They have been kneeling against the row of chairs that line the wall, according to their precedence, ranging from the Cook at one end to the Butler at the other; and they consist of the Cook, obese, elderly and respectable, Mrs. Insoley’s Maid, two Housemaids, the Kitchenmaid, the Footman, and Moore the butler. When they have scrambled to their feet they pause for a moment to gather themselves together, and, headed by the Cook, walk out. The Butler takes the Bible and the prayer-book off the table and carries them away. Claude gets up. He takes up his letters and the Times, which he puts under his arm.
I didn’t see Grace’s maid, Claude.
I dare say Grace couldn’t spare her.
If Grace were more punctual she wouldn’t be obliged to deprive her maid of the pleasure and the duty of attending morning prayers.
I didn’t see your maid either, Miss Vernon.
A Papist, Helen? Isn’t that very risky?
Aren’t you afraid she’ll corrupt the other servants?
[With a smile.] She’s a highly respectable person of well over forty.
She must be very flighty. I would as soon have an atheist.
I would never dream of having a Romish maid myself.
Is there any likelihood of your having a maid at all, Louisa?
In that case I can’t quite see what is the use of your having an opinion on the subject.
[Looking up from his letters, with a smile.] Miss Hall was only making a general reflection.
I don’t like general reflections at the breakfast table.

[During the next few speeches the Butler and the Footman come in with covered entrée dishes which they put on the sideboard, coffee and milk in silver pots, and tea. They go out. Claude retires to the window to read his letters.
I suppose you have prayers at Foley, Helen?
I’m afraid I don’t. It makes me feel rather shy to read them.
I don’t see why it should. It doesn’t make me feel shy.
You read them so well, Mrs. Insoley.
I never forget while I’m reading them that I’m a woman of birth and a woman of property.
And then I always think the servants hate them.

The more they hate them, the better it is for them. That is life, my dear Helen. It’s a very good thing to begin the day by making it distinctly understood that masters are masters and servants are servants.
And I think servants like that, Mrs. Insoley.
It is not a matter of interest to me if they like it or not, Louisa. I have the authority of my maker for it, and that is quite enough for me.
When breakfast’s at ten o’clock I cannot imagine why people shouldn’t be punctual.
Neither can I. [Going to the sideboard.] Let’s have a look at the food.
See if there’s anything I’d like, Louisa.
[Taking off the covers.] There’s fried sole—eggs and bacon.
The staple of every middle-class hotel in the kingdom.
I’ll begin with fried sole, and then I’ll have eggs and bacon, Louisa.
[Coming forward.] Oh, I’m sorry. Is there anything I can get you?
[Chaffing her fellow-guest.] And then, if Mr. Cobbett has left any, perhaps I’ll see if I can eat a devilled kidney.
[With a chuckle.] Mr. Cobbett thinks he’ll have to look nippy to get anything at all.
[To Miss Vernon.] I wonder what I can tempt you with?
I think I’ll have some fried sole.
That’s the beauty of the country. One does relish one’s breakfast, doesn’t one?
[He hands a plate to Miss Vernon, and sits down with another for himself. As he does this he takes the Times from under his arm and sits on it.
[With a smile at his peculiarity.] Is there anything in the Times, Claude?
In some ways you’re much more of a Bainbridge than an Insoley, Claude. My father used always to sit on the Times so that no one should read it before him.

I must say I don’t like to have my paper messed about by a lot of people before I’ve had a chance of looking at it. Half the pleasure of reading the Times is reading it first. Besides, the Morning Post and the Mail are on the sideboard for anyone who wants them.
Oh, I know I’m dreadfully late. Everybody’s going to scold me. And I’m so sorry.
[Imitating Mrs. Insoley.] When breakfast’s at ten o’clock I cannot imagine why people shouldn’t be punctual.
[Smiling.] Isn’t Grace down yet? [To Claude, who rises to give her something to eat.] No, don’t bother. I’ll help myself.
When I was mistress of this house breakfast was served punctually at eight o’clock every morning.
[Flippantly.] It must have seemed just like supper. Did you have it the last thing before going to bed?

I made no exceptions. The day after my cousin James broke his neck in the hunting-field and was brought to this very house on a stretcher, I came down as the clock struck. And a very hearty breakfast I ate too.
Perhaps he didn’t leave you anything.
[With a chuckle.] On the contrary, he left me all his debts.
Am I late? I think punctuality’s the most detestable of all the virtues.
It’s a royal virtue, my dear.
In that case, as a member of the middle classes, it’s not surprising that I don’t practise it.
What can I get you, darling?
Is there anything nice to eat?
[With a grim smile.] That is a matter of opinion.
There’s fried sole and eggs and bacon.
Oh, I don’t think I’ll have anything. I’ll just have some tea and toast.
My dear, you’re not off your feed, are you?
Grace has probably been stuffing herself with bread and butter in her room. I have no patience with the new-fangled custom of giving people tea when they wake up. I never give it to my guests.
Then don’t ask me to come and stay with you.
[Delighted with the opportunity he has given her.] It may surprise you, but I have no intention of doing so.
[Cheerfully.] There now. And I thought I’d made such an impression on you, Mrs. Insoley.
That’s why I couldn’t risk asking you to stay with me. Perhaps at my age I am safe from your blandishments, but Louisa is extremely susceptible.
Oh, Mrs. Insoley, how can you! Why, Mr. Cobbett must be ten years younger than I am.
I should put it at fifteen.
Don’t dash my hopes to the ground, Miss Hall. I was flattering myself you didn’t look upon me altogether with indifference.
[Archibald Insoley comes in from the garden.
Ah, I thought I’d find you still at breakfast.
We’re a lazy lot. I suppose you’ve been up and about for the last two hours.
[Looking at him.] Is anything the matter?
I thought you looked a bit odd.
A most awful thing has happened. I’ve only just heard of it.
[Getting up from his chair.] What is it, old man?

[By this time the breakfasters are disturbed; there is a certain embarrassment about them; they are suffering from the awkwardness people feel when they see some one in a condition of distress, but do not suppose it has anything to do with themselves.
You’d better come along with me to the smoking-room.
It’s too late to make a secret of it, Archibald. You’d better tell us all.
[After a moment’s hesitation.] Peggy Gann has killed herself.
[Grace springs to her feet with a cry.
[Grace comes forward, horror on her face, and walks unsteadily to a chair. She sinks into it and stares in front of her.
Why on earth did she do it?
[Going up to her, about to put his hand on her shoulder.] Grace.
[He stops and looks at her, puzzled and unhappy.
[With his eyes on Grace.] I feel I ought to do something. I don’t know what to do.
I’m afraid there’s nothing much that can be done.
I’d better go and see Gann, hadn’t I?
Won’t you finish your breakfast before you go, Claude?
Oh, I can’t eat anything more.
[Grace gets up and goes to the window.
[Almost beside herself.] For heaven’s sake, leave me alone.
[She stands with her back to the rest of the party, looking out of the window. There is a little awkward pause.
Louisa, get me some of those devilled kidneys that Mr. Cobbett has been making so much fuss about.
Louisa will get them. She likes to wait on me herself. Don’t you, Louisa?
[Miss Vernon looks as if she were going to speak to Grace, but she changes her mind and merely sits down in another chair. Every now and then she looks up at Grace.
I cannot imagine why anyone should be upset because an abandoned hussy has been so wicked as to destroy herself.
Well, it hasn’t taken my appetite away, at all events.
If we were honest with ourselves, Mr. Cobbett, we should acknowledge that nobody’s death is important enough to interfere with one’s appetite.
Oh, Mrs. Insoley, how can you say such a thing?
Louisa, I’ve been like a mother to you for ten years. Would you eat one potato less for your dinner if I were found dead in my bed to-morrow morning?
[Taking out her handkerchief.] Oh, yes, Mrs. Insoley. I really, really would.
[Touched.] You are a good girl, Louisa, and you may have that black lace shawl of mine. If you mend it carefully, it’ll last you for years.
Oh, thank you, Mrs. Insoley. You are so kind to me.
D’you think I ought to offer to go away to-day? I was going to stay till to-morrow.
I was going to-day in any case. I’m due to stay with some people in Wiltshire.
You seem to be in great demand.
I have a very pleasant fund of small talk.
I’m afraid this is not an occasion upon which you’ll find it of any use.
Come on. I’m dying for a smoke.
[She gets up and walks out through the French windows. Cobbett follows her.

[Getting up from the table.] I think you should remember, my dear Grace, that suicide is not only very wicked, but very cowardly. I have no patience with the sentimentalities of the present day. Our fathers buried people who were sinful enough to destroy themselves at the cross-roads with a stake in their insides. And it served them right.

[Grace does not answer. Mrs. Insoley, with a shrug of the shoulders, walks out of the room, followed by Miss Hall. As soon as Grace hears the door shut she turns round with an exclamation, half-smothered, of impatient anger.

Oh, did you hear? They have the heart to chatter like that when that unhappy girl is lying dead. They haven’t a word of pity. It seems to mean nothing to them that she sacrificed herself. If she died, it was to save her father, so that he shouldn’t be thrown out of work in his old age. And they call her wicked and sinful.

But is that anything new to you? Haven’t you noticed that people always rather resent the heroism of others? They don’t like the claim it makes on them, and the easiest way to defend themselves is with a sneer.
I might have saved her life if I’d chosen, but I hadn’t the courage.
[Afraid that she is going to blurt out a secret which had much better not be referred to.] Grace, don’t be stupid.
Once I suspected what she was going to do, but she was too clever for me. I so wanted to believe it was all right. I wanted her to go away quietly.

[Trying to calm her.] Lots of women have been in difficulties before, and they haven’t killed themselves. There must have been some kink in her nature. I suppose the instinct of life wasn’t so strong as it is with most of us, and—and she would have committed suicide for almost any reason.
There was only one thing to say, and I didn’t say it. I couldn’t.
My dear, for heaven’s sake pull yourself together.
D’you know why Claude was so determined she should go? Because he couldn’t bear that I should come in contact with a woman who’d done wrong.
[Looking down.] I had an idea that was at the back of his mind.
[With sudden suspicion.] Why should you know what Claude feels better than I do?
[Fearing she has given herself away.] It was a mere guess on my part.
[With a keen look at her.] When I asked you the other day whether you’d been very much in love with Claude, you wouldn’t answer.
[Smiling.] I really thought it was no business of yours.
[Gravely.] Are you in love with him still?
[Miss Vernon is about to break out indignantly, but quickly controls herself.

D’you know that my mother-in-law would give half her fortune to know—what you know? She’s been on the look-out to trip me up for years. It only wants a hint, and she can be trusted to make the most of it.
My dear, I haven’t a notion what you’re talking about.
[With a shrug of the shoulders.] How did you find out?
[Miss Vernon looks at her for a moment, then looks away in embarrassment.
I suspected before. In those circumstances hardly any men seem able to help a sort of proprietary air. He rather gave it away, you know.... And then yesterday I felt quite certain.
I’m in your hands. What are you going to do?
My dear, what can I do? Claude wouldn’t love me more because he loved you less.
No.... I feel awfully sorry for Claude.
[Almost jealously.] Claude’s your first thought always.
He’s been the whole world to me since I was a girl of sixteen.
Is that why you never married?
I never dreamt that anyone could care for Claude like that. I suppose you see something in him that I’ve never seen.... He has a hundred different ways of getting on my nerves.
You see, I’m not irritated by the mannerisms that irritate you.
[Reflectively.] Real love accepts them, I suppose.
It wants them even because it’s something individual to cling to.... And then it laughs at them a little, and the best love of all includes a sense of humour.
It’s made me feel so strange to know that you love him, Helen. It’s given him something that he’s never had before.
I don’t suppose any woman likes her husband less because she knows that another woman is eating her heart out for him.
[Slowly.] I wonder if I’ve misjudged him all these years.... D’you think I found him shallow because there was no depth in me, and narrow because I was narrow myself.
[Enter Claude Insoley. Grace turns to him quickly.
[Touching the bell.] No, he wasn’t at the cottage. I’ve sent for him and told him to come here.
They know where he is then?
Yes, worse luck. He’s been soaking at the public-house since it opened.
Peggy, d’you mean? She did it last night.
Last night? But why have we only just heard of it?
[Deeply discouraged.] Because they don’t come to us any more when they’re in trouble. They keep it to themselves.
Oh, Moore, when Gann comes let me know. I’ll come and see him at once.
Is he? I didn’t expect him yet. All right.
Won’t you let him come here, Claude? I should like to speak to him too.
I don’t think you’d better see him if he’s been drinking. He may be going to make himself rather objectionable.
I must say to him what I’ve got on my heart, Claude.
Very well. [To Moore.] Tell Gann to come here.
I dare say you’d like me to leave you.
[With a shake of the head and a smile Miss Vernon goes out. Claude looks a little uncertainly at his wife. He seeks for something to say.
What a nice woman that is! I can’t imagine why Archibald doesn’t hurry up and marry her.
Perhaps he’s not in love with her.
Any man in his senses would be in love with her.

[Grace does not answer, but she gives him a curious glance. Moore opens the door to show Gann in. Gann is dishevelled and untidy, his face haggard and drawn. He is not exactly drunk, but he is stupefied, partly with liquor and partly with grief. He carries his gun. He comes in, his cap on his head, and stands clumsily near the door.
[Gann looks at him unsteadily and slowly takes off his cap.
Did you want to speak to me, Squire?
I’ve just been round to your cottage, Gann. I saw Peggy.... I want to tell you how awfully sorry I am for what’s happened. I can never forgive myself.
[Gann steps forward with a lurch and faces Claude.
What d’you want me for? Couldn’t you let me be? D’you still want me to go?
No. That’s what I wanted to tell you.
Give us time and we’ll clear. We don’t want long. Give us time to bury the girl. That’s all we want.
I hope you’ll stay. I want to do everything I can to make up for your loss. I want you to know that I blame myself most awfully.
Will that bring ’er back to life, d’you think?
I’d give anything for this horrible accident not to have happened. [With a look at Grace.] I’m afraid it’s my fault.
She killed ’erself so as I shouldn’t be turned off. That’s why she killed ’erself. You’re a hard master—you always was. She thought it was the only way to save me from the work’us.
[Very awkwardly.] In future I’ll try to be different. I didn’t think I was hard. I thought I was only just.
I thought I was only doing my duty.
She was a good girl, after all, Squire, a good girl.
It’s easy enough for you people to keep straight. You don’t ’ave temptations like we ’ave.
No, that’s true enough. I suppose it’s not really very hard for us to be moderately decent.
[In a choking voice.] Where is the child now, Gann?
[Violently.] D’you want that too? Ain’t you satisfied yet? Has the child got to go before I stay?
No, no. I only wanted to know if there was anything I could do. I wanted to help you.
I don’t want your ’elp. I only want you to let me work and earn my wages.
That you shall do, I promise you.
Can I go now? I’ve got a deal to do this morning.
Yes.... Will you shake hands with me before you go?
I can only repeat that I’m most awfully sorry. I’m afraid there’s absolutely nothing I can do to make up for your great loss.... You can go now.
[Gann turns to go, while Claude and Grace watch him silently. Suddenly he comes back and thrusts his gun into Claude’s hand.
Look ’ere, Squire, you take my gun. I ain’t fit to keep it.
Last night when the liquor was in me I swore I’d blow your brains out and swing for it. Don’t let me ’ave the gun. I’m not fit to keep it yet. If I get on the drink again I’ll kill you.
What the dickens d’you mean by speaking to me like that! Of course you must have your gun. I can’t allow you to neglect your work.
[Almost in a whisper.] Claude, take care.
[Looking at the lock.] Why isn’t it loaded?
They took the cartridges out. I was about mad, and I don’t know what I said. If I’d come across you then—you wouldn’t be standing where you are now.
[Grace and Gann both look at him. Grace gives a start when she realises what he is going to do.
[Claude nods and goes to the door. He hesitates, with a look at Grace.
[He goes out. In a moment he comes back with two cartridges. He puts them in the gun, and hands it back to the gamekeeper.
Here you are. I don’t think I’m afraid. I’ll take my chance of your wanting to shoot me.

[Gann takes the gun, and his hands close round it convulsively. He half raises it. Claude goes to the door through which he has just come, and closes it. Then, almost mastered by the temptation, Gann pulls himself together and advances a step towards his master. Grace gives a stifled cry. Claude turns round and faces the man.
That’ll do, Gann. I don’t think I have anything more to say to you. You can go.
[Gann struggles to command himself. His fingers itch to shoot, but Claude’s unconcern prevents him.
[He turns round to go, and flings the gun violently from him.
[The man stops, looks at his master, and then, cowed, picks it up. He lurches heavily out of the room. There is a pause. Grace draws a long breath.
I’m glad you did that, Claude.
[Thinking she refers to his attempts at apology.] It was very difficult to know what to say to him.
I didn’t mean that. I meant, I’m glad you made him take the gun.
Oh! Hang it all, you didn’t think I was likely to be frightened of one of my own servants, did you?
[In a low voice.] I was rather afraid he was going to shoot you.
So was I. But I felt pretty sure he saw two of me, and I thought he’d probably shoot at the wrong one.
Rot! [He hesitates for a moment.] Grace, I’m afraid you think I’ve been an awful skunk.
[With a quick look at him.] We none of us knew anything like this was going to happen.
I’ve been feeling such an awful cad. If I’d only done what you wanted me to, this wouldn’t have happened.
That’s not your fault. I didn’t say—what I should have said to make you change your mind.

It rather put my back up that you should be so set on letting Peggy stay. But it struck me afterwards, of course you couldn’t feel the same about it as I did. I think if one’s awfully straight, one’s full of charity, don’t you know.
My dear Claude, you talk as if I were a girl of eighteen.
I don’t suppose you remember, but when Archibald told us, I wanted to say something to you....
Yes, your first thought was for me, wasn’t it?
[Going on.] And I came near you. And—and you sort of shuddered, and said: “For God’s sake, don’t touch me!”
I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to be unkind.
